strengths: Introduces a technically sound and novel formulation of symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching over Lie groups, unifying discrete and continuous symmetry discovery (including reflections via a complex-domain extension) within one framework, with a careful derivation of the target vector field on the group and its pushforward to data space (Appendix A).

Provides a rigorous and illuminating diagnostic study of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon: the paper isolates the effect in a simplified SO(2)->C4 scalar setting, computes and visualizes the posterior p(x1|xt) and its entropy, and shows the underlying cause (symmetric averaging over target modes). This kind of honest failure-mode analysis is a genuine scientific contribution beyond just a working method.

Empirically outperforms the LieGAN baseline by a substantial margin on Wasserstein-1 distance across all 2D and 3D experiments (Tables 1-2), and the proposed power-law time-scheduling fix is shown to meaningfully improve results (enabling recovery of the octahedral group where uniform-time sampling failed).

Extensive supplementary experiments (multi-object datasets, non-uniform/Gaussian structure-preserving SO(2) rotations) that test some generality of the approach beyond the core toy setups, along with many auxiliary visualizations that aid interpretability of the learned flows.

Clear and candid discussion of limitations, including failure to discover the icosahedral group even after the time-schedule fix, and open questions about scaling to noisy/real data and higher-dimensional or non-compact groups.
weaknesses: All experiments are restricted to small, synthetic, noise-free 2D/3D point clouds of hand-crafted canonical objects; there is no evaluation on real-world data or on any downstream task (e.g., plugging discovered symmetries into an equivariant network), leaving the practical significance and scalability of the method largely untested.

The method still requires a priori specification of the hypothesis group G (SO(2), GL(2,R)+, GL(2,C), SO(3)) and its dimensionality/type, which somewhat undercuts the claim of requiring 'fewer assumptions' than prior work -- the user must still guess the right ambient group family before running the method.

A core limitation (failure on higher-order finite subgroups such as octahedral without the fix, and icosahedral even with the fix) is not resolved, only characterized; the proposed power-schedule heuristic is an ad hoc empirical patch (chosen skewness n=5) rather than a principled solution, and it is unclear how it would generalize to arbitrary/larger groups.
Quantitative results lack any measure of variance (error bars/multiple seeds), and only a single baseline (LieGAN) is compared against, with limited detail on baseline hyperparameter tuning fairness.
Architectures used are simple MLPs without ablation on architecture choices, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to network capacity, sample size, or number of ODE integration steps.

The method's outputs converge to the 'closest group element in the orbit' rather than reconstructing an unbiased distribution over the true stabilizer subgroup; this behavior is noted but its implications for correctness of symmetry discovery (versus merely nearest-neighbor matching under the sampled prior transformation) are not fully analyzed theoretically.

strengths: The core idea of casting symmetry discovery as flow matching over a hypothesis Lie group (rather than operating in data space) is a reasonably novel combination of flow matching and Lie-theoretic machinery, with a careful derivation of the target vector field via exponential curves, left-invariant metrics, and the orbit-stabilizer pushforward (Appendix A).

The identification and analysis of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon is a genuinely interesting empirical observation, supported by a clean, interpretable toy experiment (SO(2) to C4 on scalar group elements) with posterior entropy and velocity-field visualizations that convincingly explain why symmetric target modes cause near-zero vector fields until late in the flow.

LieFlow substantially outperforms the LieGAN baseline on Wasserstein-1 distance across nearly all reported 2D and 3D experiments, and the paper includes a reasonably extensive appendix with additional experiments (multi-object datasets, non-uniform/structure-preserving SO(2) symmetry) that add some robustness to the core claims.
The paper is transparent about its own failure modes (octahedral group requiring a special schedule, icosahedral group failing outright), which is commendable honesty rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: All experiments are on small, synthetic, noise-free 2D/3D point clouds of hand-designed canonical shapes; despite motivating the work with physics, chemistry, and vision applications, there is no experiment on real-world or higher-dimensional data, and no demonstration that discovered symmetries actually improve downstream task performance or sample efficiency, which was a central motivating claim in the introduction.

The method fails on exactly the harder cases that matter most for demonstrating generality: it cannot discover the octahedral group without an ad hoc power time-schedule, and still fails entirely on the icosahedral group, undermining the claim that the method is 'more flexible' and requires 'fewer assumptions' than prior work.

The hypothesis group G must still be manually chosen and is restricted to simple compact groups (SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)) in experiments; scaling to larger, higher-dimensional, or non-compact groups is explicitly left to future work, which significantly narrows the practical scope relative to the stated contributions.

The proposed power time-schedule fix is a heuristic without theoretical justification tied to the group structure (e.g., why n=5, or how it should scale with group order/complexity is unclear), and the paper does not explore principled alternatives (e.g., the Riemannian diffusion approaches mentioned only as future work).

Comparison is limited to a single baseline (LieGAN); no empirical comparison is made to the closest related work (Allingham et al. 2024) or to Sherry & Smets (2025), despite both being discussed at length in related work as directly comparable methods.

The generation procedure does not reliably reconstruct the identity transformation (samples converge to the 'closest' group element rather than the true one), which is acknowledged but not quantitatively characterized—it's unclear how often/by how much this deviates and what practical impact this has.

Architecture and experimental setup are minimal (3-layer MLPs), and it's unclear whether findings (e.g., last-minute convergence, the time-schedule fix) generalize to more complex network architectures or larger-scale problems.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation of symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching on Lie groups, where the network predicts Lie algebra elements rather than data-space velocities, and the discovered subgroup emerges as the support/concentration of a learned distribution over a hypothesis group.

Rigorous derivation (Appendix A) connecting exponential-curve interpolants on the group to the induced data-space target vector field via the orbit map and its pushforward, handling the stabilizer subgroup carefully.

A genuinely interesting empirical/scientific finding: the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon, where the posterior over target modes stays near-uniform until very late in the flow due to the symmetric arrangement of modes. This is carefully diagnosed via a simplified scalar SO(2)->C4 experiment with explicit posterior/entropy computation and velocity phase portraits, which is a nice piece of analysis beyond simply reporting results.
A practical, simple fix (power-law time schedule) is proposed and shown to extend the range of discoverable groups (enabling octahedral group discovery that previously failed).

Reasonably broad empirical validation across 2D (C4, D4 including a complex-domain formulation for reflections) and 3D (Tet, Oct, SO(2)) settings, plus appendix experiments on multi-object datasets and non-uniform (structure-preserving) symmetry distributions, showing some generality.
Quantitative comparison against LieGAN baseline using Wasserstein-1 distance shows consistent and often large improvements.
Honest limitations section that explicitly reports failure modes (icosahedral group, real-world/noisy data untested) rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: All experiments are on small, synthetic, noise-free point clouds of simple canonical shapes; no real-world data or more complex domains (e.g., images used by closely related Allingham et al. 2024) are tested, limiting evidence for practical significance.

The method still assumes a known hypothesis group a priori (SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)) with a fixed parameterization/compactness, so the claimed 'fewer assumptions' relative to prior work is somewhat overstated; scaling to larger or non-compact groups is explicitly left to future work.

Core scalability limitation is unresolved: the method fails outright on the icosahedral group (60 elements) even with the proposed schedule fix, and succeeds on the octahedral group only after this post-hoc intervention, raising doubts about general applicability to more complex symmetry structures.

Empirical comparison is limited to a single baseline (LieGAN); other closely related and discussed methods (e.g., Allingham et al. 2024, Sherry & Smets 2025, Dehmamy et al. 2021) are not empirically compared despite being discussed at length in related work, making it harder to assess relative significance of the contribution.

No analysis of computational cost/training time versus baselines, sensitivity to network architecture, or robustness to noise, which would be important for assessing practical reproducibility and usefulness.

Algorithm 3's procedure for producing group elements h=Mg is motivated mostly empirically; the paper acknowledges x'_1 does not always match x1 and that the method converges to the closest mode, but a fuller theoretical characterization of when/why this yields a faithful element of H is not given.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reframing of symmetry discovery as distribution learning (support recovery) on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, rather than estimating generators directly — this naturally accommodates both continuous and discrete symmetries in one framework, which prior works (LieGAN, Allingham et al.) could not do cleanly.

The identification of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete subgroups is a genuine and interesting empirical/theoretical observation, supported by careful analysis (entropy of posterior, velocity phase portraits, toy SO(2)→C4 experiments in Appendix D). The proposed power time-schedule fix is simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated via an ablation over skewness.

Reasonably rigorous derivation of the target vector field on Lie groups (Appendix A), connecting group-valued interpolants to data-space velocities via pushforward operators, which grounds the method beyond just heuristic engineering.

Broad and fairly systematic experimental suite: 2D (SO(2), GL(2)+ with two prior parameterizations), 3D synthetic (Tet, Oct, Ico, SO(2) subgroups), and real-world ModelNet10 objects, plus tests of partial symmetry observation and robustness to masked/incomplete point clouds.

Substantial and consistent quantitative improvements over the LieGAN baseline on discrete symmetry groups (often an order of magnitude lower Wasserstein-1 distance), with comparable performance on continuous groups, and much faster training time than LieGAN.
weaknesses: Only one baseline (LieGAN) is empirically compared, despite Allingham et al. (2024) being described as the other most closely related work; without this comparison, it is hard to assess how much of the improvement is specific to LieFlow's design versus general benefits of a more flexible generative approach.

Results appear sensitive to the choice of prior/parameterization over the hypothesis group — e.g., GL(2)+ Lie-algebra-coefficient sampling gives W1=1.321 while matrix-composition sampling gives 0.428 for the same target C4 group — which is in some tension with the abstract's claim of not assuming 'a specific distribution over the group elements'; this sensitivity and its implications are not deeply analyzed.

Datasets are small in scale (single canonical shapes per experiment, 128-point clouds, low-dimensional hypothesis groups SO(2)/GL(2)/SO(3)); the paper does not demonstrate scalability to higher-dimensional or more complex data/groups, which the authors acknowledge but which materially limits the significance of the contribution.

Experiments largely lack variance/error bars or multiple-seed reporting for the main quantitative tables (Tables 1–3), making it difficult to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements over LieGAN.

The method still requires specifying a hypothesis group G a priori (with connectedness and often compactness assumptions for the prior/logarithm map to be well-defined), which somewhat undercuts the framing of fully automatic, assumption-free symmetry discovery relative to prior work criticized for similar requirements.

The partial-symmetry handling (Section 4.3) is introduced with reasonable theoretical motivation but tested only on a single, simple synthetic case (C4 arrow with 3 of 4 rotations observed), leaving open how well this generalizes to more complex partial-symmetry settings.

strengths: The core reformulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching is conceptually appealing and elegantly sidesteps the need to fix a Lie algebra basis or a specific coefficient distribution, as required by LieGAN and other prior works.

The derivation of the target Lie-algebra vector field via left-invariant exponential interpolants (Appendix A) is carried out with reasonable rigor and connects cleanly to the orbit-stabilizer structure of the group action.

The identification and analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete symmetry groups is a genuinely useful empirical/diagnostic contribution, supported by posterior-entropy analysis (Appendix D) and a simple, effective fix (power time schedule) with a clear ablation over the skewness parameter.

Experiments span a reasonable range of settings (2D/3D synthetic point clouds, ModelNet10, partial symmetries, masked/incomplete observations), and the method shows large quantitative improvements over LieGAN on discrete-group discovery tasks as measured by Wasserstein-1 distance.
weaknesses: Only one baseline (LieGAN) is empirically compared, despite the paper explicitly identifying Allingham et al. (2024) as 'most related' to this work; no quantitative or qualitative comparison to that method (or to Ko et al., Shaw et al., or other symmetry-discovery baselines) is provided, which weakens the significance claims.

In Table 1, LieGAN's reported Wasserstein-1 distances are essentially identical across the SO(2)→C4, GL(2)+→C4(L), and GL(2)+→C4(M) columns (1.688/1.672 repeated verbatim), which strongly suggests the baseline is not learning anything useful or was not properly tuned/adapted to the different hypothesis groups, undermining confidence in the comparative claims of 'significant improvement.'

The method still requires substantial prior knowledge — the family of the hypothesis group (SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)) must be specified in advance — which is in tension with the framing of 'automatic' symmetry discovery 'without domain expertise'; the actual discovery is restricted to finding a subgroup within a manually chosen group family.

No statistical rigor: all quantitative results (Tables 1-3) appear to be single-run point estimates without error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess robustness or significance of the reported gaps.

The theoretical justification for why the flow-matching objective 'filters out' non-symmetric transformations (Section 4.1) is informal and heuristic ('transformations that do not preserve the data distribution produce inconsistent targets...which cancel out'), with no formal proposition, theorem, or convergence guarantee backing the central claim that the learned distribution concentrates on the true symmetry group H.

Handling of partially observed symmetries (Section 4.3) is explored only in a single toy 2D example (three arrow orientations); the conditional distribution pθ(·|x) that is central to this generalization is never actually demonstrated as being learned/conditioned on x in the reported experiments, leaving this claimed capability largely unvalidated.

The Riemannian metric G used in the CFM loss (Eq. 5) is left abstract in the main text and only becomes concrete implicitly via implementation choices; sensitivity of results to this metric choice is not analyzed, despite it plausibly affecting both training dynamics and the fairness of comparisons to LieGAN.

Downstream utility claims in the conclusion (e.g., 'offering improved sample efficiency and generalization for downstream tasks') are speculative and not empirically demonstrated anywhere in the paper — there is no integration of discovered symmetries into an equivariant network or downstream task evaluation.

Scale of experiments is limited to small point clouds (128 points) and simple MLP/2-layer Transformer architectures; no evidence is given that the approach extends to more complex real-world domains (e.g., molecular or physical systems) that motivate the introduction, despite the paper's emphasis on such applications.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning (support estimation) on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, rather than the generator-estimation paradigm used in most prior work (LieGAN, Benton et al., Allingham et al.).

The framework genuinely unifies continuous and discrete symmetry discovery without requiring a fixed Lie algebra basis or a hand-chosen prior over coefficients (e.g., multi-modal delta mixtures needed by LieGAN for discrete groups), which is a real practical limitation the paper addresses convincingly.

Rigorous derivation of the conditional flow-matching objective on Lie groups (Appendix A), including a careful treatment of the pushforward from the group tangent space to the data tangent space via the orbit map and stabilizer considerations.

The identification of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete subgroups is an interesting and non-obvious empirical/theoretical finding, supported by a careful diagnostic study (posterior entropy analysis, velocity phase portraits, Bayes-rule posterior derivation) rather than just an ad hoc observation.

The proposed power time-scheduling fix is simple, cheap, and clearly ablated (Table 4, Figure 15), directly addressing the diagnosed failure mode and showing consistent improvement, notably enabling recovery of the challenging icosahedral group.

Broad and reasonably thorough experimental suite: 2D synthetic (multiple hypothesis groups/priors), 3D synthetic (four target groups), real-world ModelNet10, partial symmetry setting, and robustness to incomplete/masked observations — going beyond the toy settings common in this literature.
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithms (1-4), full training/architecture details in the appendix, and disclosed LLM usage.
weaknesses: Only one baseline (LieGAN) is quantitatively compared, despite the paper explicitly identifying Allingham et al. (2024) as equally 'most related' work with a similar distributional viewpoint; omitting this comparison leaves open whether LieFlow's advantages are specific to LieGAN's adversarial/fixed-prior limitations rather than a general advance over the state of the art.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported in Tables 1-3, making it hard to assess the reliability of the reported Wasserstein-1 improvements, especially in cases where LieFlow only marginally beats or slightly underperforms LieGAN (e.g., SO(3)→SO(2)(a) on ModelNet10, where LieGAN is actually better: 0.0291 vs 0.0461).

Gains over LieGAN are 'comparable' rather than clearly superior for continuous groups; the paper's headline improvement is specifically for discrete groups, so the claimed general superiority of the unified framework is only partially borne out empirically.

The claim of a fully 'unified' framework is somewhat undercut by the need for a different (power) time-scheduling hyperparameter specifically tuned for discrete/high-order groups (e.g., icosahedral) — the method is not hyperparameter-agnostic across the continuous/discrete spectrum.

The approach fundamentally requires the user to specify a hypothesis group G presumed to contain the true H; the paper does not explore what happens when this assumption is violated (model misspecification), nor systematically study sensitivity to the choice/size of G beyond a few small cases (SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)).

Experiments remain small-scale (small point clouds, limited objects per category, low-dimensional Lie groups up to SO(3)/GL(2)); the authors acknowledge this, but the significance of the contribution for more complex or higher-dimensional real-world settings (e.g., non-compact groups, higher-dimensional representations) remains untested.

The Wasserstein-1 metric aggregates over generated vs. ground-truth group elements but does not directly measure calibration/coverage of the full learned distribution (e.g., mode-collapse vs. proper multimodality), so some qualitative claims (accurate concentration on H) rely mainly on visual inspection of histograms/Mollweide plots rather than a distributional divergence metric.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reframing of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, avoiding the fixed Lie-algebra-basis/coefficient-distribution assumptions of prior work (LieGAN, Augerino, SGM).
Genuinely unifies discovery of continuous and discrete (and partially observed) symmetries within one framework; prior methods are typically specialized to one regime.

Solid theoretical grounding: careful derivation of the conditional target vector field via group interpolants (Appendix A), explicit discussion of stabilizer-induced degeneracy, and a clearly-stated support-recovery theorem (Prop. 4.1 / Theorem B.4) with transparent assumptions.

Identification and analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups is an interesting and non-obvious empirical/theoretical observation, supported by posterior-entropy analysis (Appendix E), and the proposed power time-schedule fix is validated with an ablation (Table 4, Fig. 17).

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental suite: 2D/3D synthetic data, ModelNet10, and a real-world MI-Motion dataset, plus robustness experiments under masking/noise and partial-symmetry settings, with consistent and often large improvements over LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino on discrete groups while remaining competitive on continuous groups.
Good reproducibility support: detailed training/architecture details in Appendix D, explicit algorithms (1-3), and extensive supplementary visualizations.
weaknesses: The MI-Motion 'real-world' evaluation is only qualitative (histograms); no quantitative metric (e.g., W1/RI) is reported there since ground-truth symmetry is unknown, so the central quantitative claims of accurate discovery are not verified in the one genuinely real-world setting.

The evaluation protocol (Wasserstein-1 distance to ground-truth group elements) requires known ground-truth symmetry generators, which is only available by construction in the synthetic/ModelNet10 settings; this limits generalizability of the evaluation methodology to more realistic use cases where the paper's own motivation (unknown symmetries) applies.

LieGAN comparisons in Table 1 report identical W1 values across different hypothesis groups for LieGAN 'since it does not depend on hypothesis groups,' which makes the baseline comparison somewhat structurally different from LieFlow's setup and could be seen as advantaging the proposed method's normalized RI metric rather than a fully matched comparison.

No downstream evaluation demonstrating that discovered symmetries actually improve sample efficiency or performance in equivariant models, despite this being a primary motivation stated in the introduction/abstract.

Theorem 4.1/B.4 relies on strong idealized assumptions (perfect FM convergence, globally generated support, point stabilizers being global symmetries) that are unlikely to hold exactly in practice, and the paper itself notes these can fail under partial/approximate symmetries — the practical predictive value of the theorem for real applications is therefore limited.

Requires a priori specification of the hypothesis group G (SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)), which remains a nontrivial limitation shared with prior work, and scaling to larger/non-compact/high-dimensional hypothesis groups is left as future work without empirical exploration beyond the tested cases.

strengths: The core idea of reframing symmetry discovery as learning a distribution over a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching (rather than fixing a Lie algebra basis/coefficient distribution as in LieGAN or learning explicit canonicalization as in SGM) is a reasonable and somewhat novel unification of continuous and discrete symmetry discovery.

The paper provides a rigorous (if assumption-heavy) theoretical treatment: a derivation of the conditional target vector field on Lie groups (Appendix A) and a formal proposition with explicit assumptions and proof (Appendix B) characterizing when the sampled group elements are supported in the true symmetry group H.

The identification and analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete subgroups is an interesting empirical observation, backed by posterior-entropy and velocity-field analyses (Section 5.4, Appendix E), and the proposed power time-schedule is shown to meaningfully fix the Ico recovery failure.

Experiments span a reasonably broad range of settings (2D/3D synthetic point clouds, ModelNet10, real-world MI-Motion, partial/functional symmetries, noise robustness), and LieFlow shows large improvements over LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino specifically on discrete symmetry groups while remaining competitive on continuous ones.
weaknesses: The method still requires the user to manually specify a hypothesis Lie group G (SO(2), GL(2)+, SO(3)) that must already contain the true symmetry as a subgroup, which substantially limits the claimed 'automatic' discovery; the paper does not show how to select or grow G when little is known a priori, nor test genuinely unknown/mixed group families beyond rotations.

The quantitative metric (Wasserstein distance to known ground-truth group elements) is only applicable when the true symmetry group is known, which is true for all synthetic/ModelNet10 experiments; for the only real-world dataset without an imposed ground truth (MI-Motion), evaluation is purely qualitative (histograms), so the central claims of 'real-world' applicability are not quantitatively substantiated.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfavorable to LieGAN for discrete groups: the paper's own related-work discussion notes LieGAN can discover discrete groups if given a carefully chosen multi-modal delta-mixture prior, but the experiments only use a uniform/Gaussian coefficient prior, which could understate LieGAN's best achievable performance and make the 'significant improvement on discrete symmetries' framing somewhat self-serving.

Proposition 4.1's guarantee depends on three fairly strong, difficult-to-verify assumptions (ideal convergence, globally generated support with a single global H shared across all orbits, and point stabilizers already being global symmetries); the 'globally generated support' assumption explicitly concedes failure under mixed/local symmetries, which is common in real data, so the theory offers limited practical assurance beyond the idealized synthetic settings tested.

No downstream evaluation demonstrates that the discovered symmetries are actually useful (e.g., improving sample efficiency or accuracy of an equivariant model built from the discovered H), leaving the practical significance of the contribution largely unconfirmed and relegated to 'future work.'

The method's scalability beyond small, well-known matrix Lie groups (SO(2), SO(3), GL(2)+) is untested; higher-dimensional, non-compact, or product groups relevant to many real applications are not explored, despite being flagged as a known limitation.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel reframing of symmetry discovery as distribution learning over a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, which elegantly unifies discrete and continuous symmetry discovery within a single framework without requiring a fixed Lie algebra basis or prescribed coefficient distribution (a clear advance over LieGAN, Augerino, SGM).

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: 2D synthetic point clouds with two hypothesis groups (SO(2), GL(2)+) and two sampling strategies, 3D synthetic tetrahedra with four target groups, real-object ModelNet10 with five target groups, and a genuinely real-world motion-capture dataset (MI-Motion) where the ground-truth symmetry is not imposed but discovered. Results consistently show large improvements over LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino on discrete symmetries while matching them on continuous ones.

The identification of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups is an interesting and well-supported empirical/analytical finding (posterior entropy analysis, velocity phase portraits), and the proposed power time-scheduling fix is simple, well-ablated (Table 4, Figure 17), and clearly improves results (e.g., enabling icosahedral group recovery).

A theoretical support-recovery result (Theorem B.4) is provided with explicitly stated assumptions, giving some principled grounding to the empirical method, and the authors are transparent about when assumptions may fail (e.g., partial/approximate symmetries, continuous stabilizers).

Good supplementary analyses: robustness to noise/masking, partially observed symmetry settings (both input-conditional and functional partial symmetry), and a non-trivial stabilizer experiment (rectangle with C2 self-symmetry) addressing a subtle identifiability concern.
Reasonably reproducible: detailed training/architecture/hyperparameter descriptions in the appendix, and a clear algorithmic presentation (Algorithms 1–3).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Theorem B.4) rests on fairly strong, somewhat idealized assumptions (ideal convergence to the global optimum, globally generated support, point stabilizers already being global symmetries) that are unlikely to hold exactly in practice, and are explicitly acknowledged to fail precisely in the partial/approximate-symmetry regime that the paper otherwise emphasizes as an application (e.g., MI-Motion). The practical value of the theorem for the messier experimental settings is therefore limited.

The method still requires the user to specify a hypothesis group G a priori (e.g., SO(2), GL(2)+, SO(3)), which somewhat tempers the claim of fully 'automatic' symmetry discovery; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not explore how performance degrades with increasingly uninformative or higher-dimensional hypothesis groups beyond the cases tested.

All demonstrated discrete/continuous symmetries are essentially rotation subgroups (finite point groups of SO(3), SO(2) subgroups, C4, and GL(2)+ affine examples); the framework is not tested on translations, permutations, or richer non-compact/higher-dimensional Lie groups, so the claimed generality to arbitrary matrix Lie groups is not fully empirically substantiated.

The MI-Motion real-world experiment lacks a quantitative evaluation against ground truth (no Wasserstein-distance table, unlike the other experiments), relying only on qualitative histogram comparison against LieGAN, which weakens the strength of the claimed real-world validation.

The entropy/posterior analysis in Appendix E that motivates the last-minute convergence explanation is conducted in a simplified 1D scalar group setting; while illustrative, it is not rigorously shown to carry over quantitatively to the higher-dimensional matrix Lie group settings used in the main experiments.

The method does not recover explicit algebraic structure (generators, group presentation) of the discovered symmetry, limiting downstream interpretability/usability compared to generator-based approaches, as acknowledged by the authors.
